add_eyes.name: Franz Schubert
add_eyes.role: Composer, aged 27; ill, short of money and living in Vienna
add_eyes.side: Viennese composers of the next generation
add_eyes.vantage_label: the next generation, watching from the same city
add_eyes.authenticity: Letter to Leopold Kupelwieser in Rome, 31 March 1824; printed in O. E. Deutsch, Schubert: Die Dokumente seines Lebens. The tradition that Schubert attended the premiere on 7 May is often repeated but is not supported by a dated document of his own.
add_eyes.bio: Five weeks before the premiere Schubert passed on the news of Beethoven's concert to a friend abroad and set out his own plan: chamber works first, then a large symphony. The letter shows a younger composer measuring himself against the event before it happened.

sources.title: WPR: Schubert, down on his luck (letter of 31 March 1824)
Interlude: the rediscovery of Schubert's 'Great' C major Symphony

add_eyes.name: Philharmonic Society of London (directors' minutes)
add_eyes.role: Concert society of professional musicians; commissioner and first foreign performer of the symphony
add_eyes.where: London; concerts at the Argyll Rooms
add_eyes.authenticity: The Society's minute books and correspondence are in the Royal Philharmonic Society archive at the British Library. Resolutions are cited here as printed by Thayer and summarised by later studies; the minute books themselves were not consulted.
add_eyes.bio: The Society commissioned the symphony in 1822 and gave its first performance abroad in 1825. Two years later, when Beethoven was dying, its directors voted him money. Its dated resolutions frame both ends of the chapter.

add_eyes.name: London music press: The Harmonicon and the Quarterly Musical Magazine (unsigned reviews)
add_eyes.authenticity: 'Philharmonic Concerts: Third concert, Monday, March 21st', The Harmonicon 3, no. 28 (April 1825), pp. 69–70. Unsigned; it is not by Smart. Also the separate Quarterly Musical Magazine and Review 7, no. 25 (1825), pp. 80–84, filed under the same eye as the London press.
add_eyes.bio: The Harmonicon gave London's first printed verdict on the symphony a few weeks after the performance. It admired parts of it and found the whole far too long. Its view shows how the work sounded to a well-informed audience with no Viennese legend attached.

add_eyes.name: Ignaz von Seyfried
add_eyes.role: Viennese Kapellmeister and composer, aged 48; long associated with performances of Beethoven's works at the Theater an der Wien
add_eyes.side: Viennese musical establishment, writing for a Mainz journal
add_eyes.vantage_label: Viennese musician reporting to the German press
add_eyes.authenticity: Brief report in Caecilia (Mainz, Schott) 1 (June 1824), p. 200; translated in the Boston University Beethoven Center's collection of contemporary reviews. Whether he was in the hall on 7 May is not stated.
add_eyes.bio: Seyfried had worked alongside Beethoven for two decades. His short notice for the new Mainz journal Caecilia closed his account of the Viennese season with the concert. It carried the verdict of the city's connoisseurs to readers in the Rhineland.

sources.title: Critical reception of Beethoven's Opp. 123–124 (BU Beethoven Center translations)

add_entries.headline: The directors vote fifty pounds for a symphony
add_entries.digest: The Society's directors resolved to offer Beethoven fifty pounds for a manuscript symphony. The score was to arrive by the following March. Beethoven could sell it elsewhere eighteen months after London received it. Ries was asked to pass on the terms.
add_entries.source_note: Resolution of 10 November 1822 as cited by Thayer vol. III and the Wikipedia article on the British premiere

add_entries.headline: Schubert passes on the news and plans his own symphony
add_entries.digest: Writing to the painter Kupelwieser in Rome, Schubert described himself as the most wretched man alive. His operas were unwanted and he had no money. Then he passed on the city's news: Beethoven was to give a concert with a new symphony, three pieces from the new Mass and a new overture. Schubert hoped to give such a concert himself the following year, and he described his recent quartets and octet as a way of preparing for a large symphony.
add_entries.source_note: Schubert to Kupelwieser, 31 March 1824 (Deutsch, Dokumente); WPR summary of the letter; Interlude on the 'grand symphony' plan

add_entries.headline: A copy of the score goes to London's agent
add_entries.digest: Ten days before the premiere a copyist's score was handed to the Philharmonic Society's agent in Vienna to go to London. London's eighteen months of exclusive use began when it arrived. The Viennese premiere therefore went ahead with the London score already sent.
add_entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (handover to the Society's agent); day uncertain

add_entries.headline: A Kapellmeister reports the connoisseurs' verdict to the Rhineland
add_entries.digest: Seyfried's brief notice in Caecilia closed the Viennese winter season with Beethoven's concert. He wrote that connoisseurs agreed the composer had gone beyond everything he had written before. He promised a fuller account later. Unlike Kanne, he said nothing about thin rehearsals or a hall that swallowed the sound.
add_entries.source_note: Caecilia 1 (June 1824), p. 200, item 123.4 in the BU Beethoven Center translations

add_entries.headline: London's verdict: fine passages, far too long
add_entries.digest: Reviewing the Philharmonic's third concert of the season, the Harmonicon's unsigned critic complained above all of the symphony's length. He suggested that the choral finale be removed altogether. London had heard that finale sung in Italian.
add_entries.quote: it is at least twice as long as it should be
add_entries.source_note: The Harmonicon 3, no. 28 (April 1825), pp. 69–70, quoted in the Wikipedia article on the British premiere

add_entries.headline: A second London journal piles on: its weakest symphony
add_entries.digest: The Quarterly Musical Magazine and Review, another London music journal, printed a longer notice titled 'Beethoven's New Symphony'. It ranked the work the least excellent of all Beethoven's symphonies and predicted that its length would always draw complaints.
add_entries.quote: its length alone will be a never-failing cause of complaint
add_entries.source_note: Quarterly Musical Magazine and Review 7, no. 25 (1825), pp. 80–84, quoted in the Wikipedia article on the British premiere; month not verified

add_entries.headline: The directors send the dying composer one hundred pounds
add_entries.digest: Beethoven, bedridden and dictating his letters, had written to Moscheles, Smart and Stumpff asking whether the Society might help him. On receiving the letter the directors met at once and voted one hundred pounds, which was sent to Vienna through Moscheles. It was an advance against a benefit concert that never took place.
add_entries.source_note: Beethoven-Haus 'The Philharmonic Society' (immediate meeting, £100 sent); day as given by Thayer vol. III, not checked against the minute book

add_entries.headline: Thanking London and offering a tenth symphony
add_entries.digest: Eight days before his death Beethoven dictated a letter of thanks to Moscheles for the Society's money. He promised the Society a new symphony, already sketched, and an overture. The Society had commissioned the Ninth, and this letter was also addressed to London.
add_entries.source_note: Beethoven to Moscheles, 18 March 1827 (Thayer vol. III; Beethoven's Letters); not rechecked in this edition

add_convergences.label: London commissions a symphony (10 November–20 December 1822)
add_convergences.note: Three documents: a committee resolution in London, a pupil's letter carrying the terms, and the composer's grudging acceptance. The symphony began as a contract with a deadline that it then missed.

add_convergences.label: The concert in print (May–June 1824)
add_convergences.note: Kanne in Vienna blamed the hall and the rehearsals. Seyfried, writing for Mainz, passed on only the connoisseurs' verdict that Beethoven had surpassed himself. The Wiener Zeitschrift said expectations were exceeded. Readers outside Vienna got the more flattering version first.

add_convergences.label: London's last payment (February–March 1827)
add_convergences.note: The institution that commissioned the Ninth voted the dying composer one hundred pounds, and he answered by promising them another symphony. The chapter's London story ends where it began, with a resolution and a promise.

add_ties.note: Schubert reported Beethoven's coming concert in his letter of 31 March 1824 and took it as a model for one of his own. The common claim that he was in the audience on 7 May is unconfirmed.
Smart was a founding member of the Society, conducted its 1825 performance and was one of the three Londoners Beethoven wrote to for help in 1827.
Ries, a member in London, carried the Society's 1822 offer to his old teacher.
The Harmonicon reviewed Smart's performance of 21 March 1825. Its complaints about length are part of the background to Smart's journey in September 1825 to ask Beethoven about tempos.
